rv.q: “The Addams Family” looks spectacular.
But for those in love with Addams' dry sensibility, the trade-offs in banality may not be tolerable.
You'll laugh a lot, though never during the unmemorable songs, which are supposed to be funny but aren't.
The two have concocted a predictable tale of culture clashes between the oddball Addams crew and the square, straight-laced Ohio family whose son wants to marry almost grown-up Wednesday.
But $16.5 million has brought forth an ill-formed one-dimensional cartoon with lines and shading not quite inked in.
It's definitely a feat of some kind: Broadway's "The Addams Family" has watered down one of the quirkiest pop- culture creations ever.
But “Addams Family” nonetheless seems an opportunity missed, lacking the comic inspiration that would have made it more than just a family alternative to “Wicked.”
Addams’s poisoned brew is turned into Kool-Aid.
This latest reincarnation of “The Addams Family” is clearly relying, above all, on its title characters’ high recognition factor.
Oh Broadway, Broadway, Broadway. Don't you know, you never seem sadder or more imaginatively barren than when you're diving for commercial relevance in the dumpsters behind old TV shows and movies?
The result is a disappointment, sure—but mostly because this expensively produced, ideally cast show could have been so spectacular.
It's in such quieter moments that the iconic characters on stage become more than mere shtick figures.
It is reminiscent of The Producers, Spamalot, Young Frankenstein and Shrek … those shows that rely on a cascade of gags and outrageous concepts.
And a lucky thing, too, since it is Lane and Hoffman’s ace comic timing, as well as the astringent poise of Bebe Neuwirth, as the mother Morticia, that keep things palatable.
As “The Addams Family” progressed, however, my reaction changed.
Besides being unoriginal it's uncompelling to boot.
Indeed, only a handful of theatergoers are likely to find The Addams Family worth a second visit.
The jokes, however artfully executed, are seldom surprising, and making cartoon characters who worked in the context of a half-hour sitcom compelling over 2 hours proves a serious stretch.
Then the rest of the show arrives, and it's half-baked and already nibbled, starting with the two-cent story.
This "Addams Family" has been reduced to a single snap.
Even Nathan Lane's resourcefulness, Kevin Chamberlin's moonstruck charm, and Carolee Carmello's giddy vocal display can't reanimate this inert monstrosity.
Enforced by zestful players, the screwy Addams personalities fortunately prevail for most of the show.

Firmly in the ‘good rather than great’ camp of musicals, The Addams Family looks great but a weak score and thin plot don’t do its iconic characters justice, and it struggles to explore what it is that makes their popularity live on.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actor in a Musical

cn.t: Critics largely pan this ghoulish misfire—strong visuals and Lane/Neuwirth's star power can't save a weak book and forgettable score that drains the Addams' macabre charm.

vs.sum: A handsome Art Deco house with a distinctive celestial ceiling and wide auditorium. Sightlines are good from center seats but the wide layout means far-side seats lose some stage width. Notoriously narrow seats make comfort a challenge for longer shows.

acc.note: Step-free to lobby and Orchestra. Copper induction loop available. 5 wheelchair spaces.
